name: ACME Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames)

sources.note: Local PSI record data/source/psi/PSI-22.json: flightProgram 'International Space Station (ISS)'
Challenge brief, 'Hardware': the six ACME experiments were conducted with the same modular ACME hardware in the CIR on the ISS

objective.value: Gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how an electric field (acting on the ions naturally produced in the flame) can be used to control non-premixed laminar diffusion flames. Specific goals: relate electric-field voltage to chemi-ion current, analyze the dynamic flame response to electric forcing, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames.

sources.note: Local PSI record objective: understand the relationship between electric-field voltage and chemi-ion current, analyze dynamic flame response to electric-field changes, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames
NASA Science E-FIELD Flames page: gain improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the electric field can control non-premixed flames

value: fundamental

sources.note: Local PSI record researchImpacts states the E-FIELD Flames research 'is not being conducted to serve any space applications', though findings could aid future space-based combustion devices
NASA ACME document frames ACME as fundamental microgravity research; the primary goal is efficiency and reduced pollutant emission, with fire prevention only a secondary objective for the project

safety_functions.note: Classed as fundamental: E-FIELD Flames targets flame-ion physics and flame control, not a prevention/detection/suppression method. The ACME project lists a secondary spacecraft fire-prevention objective, but that is stated for the project (and chiefly for BRE), not for E-FIELD Flames itself; the PSI record explicitly says no space application is intended.

sources.note: Local PSI record approach: 'The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames'
Challenge brief, 'Hardware': all six ACME experiments featured flames of gaseous fuels

value: methane (CH4)
ethylene (C2H4)

sources.note: Local PSI record approach: 'Methane and ethylene were used as fuels and diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength'
The PSI per-test table (data/source/psi/tables/PSI-22.csv) lists fuel bottles of 100% CH4, 40% CH4, 100% C2H4 and 30% C2H4, and fuel concentrations from 25% to 100%

fuel_materials.note: Gaseous fuels methane and ethylene, diluted with nitrogen. Oxidizer is air (see conditions).

fuel_geometry.value: Gaseous non-premixed jet flames in two configurations: a gas-jet burner producing a small focused flame with no surrounding coflow, and a normal coflow flame using the same coflow burner as the CLD Flame experiment, where the fuel jet is surrounded by a weak synthetic air coflow. A flat circular copper mesh electrode is suspended downstream of the burner.

sources.note: Local PSI record approach: gas-jet burner makes a small focused flame for ion-driven convection studies; the coflow burner surrounds the fuel jet with a weak synthetic air flow for flame stability and soot analysis; tests done with and without a coflow of air

NASA ACME document: E-FIELD Flames conducted with a normal coflow flame (as in the CLD Flame experiment) or a simple gas-jet flame with no surrounding coflow; a flat circular mesh sits above the burner
Local PSI record experimentHardware: 'Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME'
Challenge brief, 'Hardware': the six ACME experiments were all conducted with the same modular ACME hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)

apparatus.value: ACME modular chamber insert in the CIR: exchangeable burner (gas-jet or the CLD coflow burner), hot-wire igniter, gas delivery with mass flow controllers, and experiment-unique hardware including a high-voltage supply and a crew-removable electrode mesh settable between +10 and -10 kV, positioned about 35 or 50 mm downstream of the insulated burner. Flame instrumentation includes radiometers, photomultiplier tubes and thin-filament pyrometry fibers.

sources.note: NASA ACME document: ACME chamber insert with exchangeable burner, hot-wire igniter, gas delivery; E-FIELD-specific high-voltage supply and crew-removable electrode mesh settable between +10 and -10 kV, mesh orthogonal to the chamber axis about 35 or 50 mm downstream of the insulated burner; ion current via voltage drop across a known resistor
Local PSI record approach: a high-voltage copper mesh electrode above the burner tip generated the electric field; high-voltage differential up to 10 kV between the burner and the mesh

o2_percent.note: No readable source states an oxygen-concentration range for E-FIELD Flames. The PSI per-test table (data/source/psi/tables/PSI-22.csv) has no O2 column (its headers are Test Type, Test Day, Year, Month, Date, Mesh Polarity, Fuel Bottle, Fuel Conc, Flames Ignited, Notes), and data/source/psi/tables/conditions.json lists null o2 for PSI-22. The 2022 foundation paper's abstract describes 'small diffusion flames of methane (in air)', implying an air-like atmosphere, but it states no numeric O2; left unknown rather than inferred.

pressure_psi.note: No readable source states a chamber-pressure range for E-FIELD Flames. PSI gives no pressure, the per-test table has no pressure column, and conditions.json lists null pressure for PSI-22. The ACME document says the experiments are constant-volume studies with the pressure allowed to rise, but gives no pressure value; left unknown.

airflow.note: PSI and the ACME document state that tests were run both with and without a coflow of air (a weak synthetic air coflow around the fuel jet) and that coflow velocity was a varied parameter, but no velocity value is given in a readable source, so it is left unknown.

sources.note: Local PSI record projectType 'Microgravity Investigation'; approach says the microgravity environment isolates electric-field effects from buoyancy forces
Challenge brief, 'Partial-gravity data': the experiment flew in microgravity and only mimics partial gravity through the electric field

gravity_g.note: True microgravity (ISS, ~0 g). IMPORTANT: E-FIELD Flames only MIMICS partial gravity via the electric field's effect on flame ions; it is not partial-gravity data. The brief states PSI currently holds no true partial-gravity combustion data.

value: nitrogen (N2)

sources.note: Local PSI record approach: methane and ethylene were 'diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength'; dilution levels were varied from highly stable to near-extinction flames

diluents.note: Nitrogen was used to dilute the fuel. The ACME chamber insert can also deliver inert gases such as helium or carbon dioxide for other ACME experiments, but nitrogen is the diluent stated for E-FIELD Flames.

relevance_notes.value: Named in the challenge brief as the experiment that only MIMICS partial gravity, through the effect of an electric field on the ions that naturally occur in flames. The brief stresses that PSI currently has no true partial-gravity combustion data, so this record must never be presented as partial-gravity data. Its relevance to crew fire safety is indirect: it clarifies how flame ions, soot and stability can be manipulated, which informs fire-behaviour modelling rather than a specific prevention, detection or suppression method.

sources.note: Challenge brief, 'Partial-gravity data': partial gravity was mimicked in ACME E-FIELD Flames through the effect of the electric field on flame ions; there is currently no partial-gravity combustion data available in PSI

value: The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion
Electric-field-assisted combustion may allow more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption as well as unwanted emissions
Improved understanding and modelling of ion-driven combustion could support soot control (soot is both useful and a health hazard)

sources.note: Local PSI record researchImpacts: electric-field flame control can reduce harmful pollutants; combustion using electric fields may allow more efficient combustion and lower fuel consumption and emissions
NASA ACME document: the primary goal of ACME is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion

notes: Sources used: the local PSI record data/source/psi/PSI-22.json and PSI-22.search.json, the PSI per-test table data/source/psi/tables/PSI-22.csv, the NASA ACME one-page document (PDF), the NASA Science E-FIELD Flames page, and the abstract of the 2022 Combustion and Flame foundation paper. The psi.nasa.gov investigation page was NOT loaded (it is JavaScript); no claim is made to have read it.

PSI data files: the PSI record's 'added' list is empty (no downloadable data files). It lists only four representative images (ACME logo.png, E-Field flames blue 2.jpg, E-Field Flames.jpg, E-Field Flames blue.jpg) and one metadata zip (PSI-22_metadata_ACME E-FIELD Flames.zip). The record reports a totalFileSize near 950 GB but exposes no per-sample data files; nothing is claimed to be available for download.

Partial gravity: E-FIELD Flames only mimics partial gravity through the electric field's action on flame ions. It is microgravity data (0 g), not true partial-gravity data. Kept accurate in gravity_g and relevance_notes.

Oxygen and pressure are left unknown. conditions.json records null o2/pressure/flow for PSI-22 and the per-test CSV is a test-log (dates, mesh polarity, fuel bottle, fuel concentration), not a conditions table. The 2022 paper abstract mentioning methane 'in air' was treated as non-numeric and not converted into an O2 value.

The ACSearch record lists related investigation PSI-23 (ACME s-Flames) and the record's own publication list includes many related electric-field papers (drop-tower and ground studies) besides the on-orbit ACME work; only the three most directly relevant are listed under publications.
